title: 2026 Sedona Mountain Bike Festival: Speed Dating Bike Demos From ASYM, Canfield, Spot, Revel, and Trek – Spencer Harding
content:
While cruising the aisle at Sedona Mountain Bike Festival can be its own vortex, escaping the vortex on a sweet demo bike is a treat. Spencer was able to sneak in rides on five unique bikes that caught his eye during his time at Sedona Mountain Bike Festival. See his quick thoughts on bikes from ASYM, Canfield, Revel, Spot, and Trek below…

In past years at Sedona Mountain Bike Festival, I got out for maybe one demo bike at best, either due to weather or time constraints. Flying solo to the weekend for the first time this year, I carved out some time to actually ride.

Each bike was ridden on the same-ish five-mile lap near the Posse Grounds consisting of Grand Central and Adobe Jack trails, with a pedal up the road to access those trails. The paved climb gave insights into pedaling behavior, and the trails had a bit of everything: short drops, steep climbs, berms, tight corners, and rocky ledges. You can only tell so much from an hour-long pedal, but that is why I’m calling it speed dating. I had an hour to let these sweet rides seduce me and wow me.

ASYM Prototype

The prototype fleet from Boulder-based ASYM was a head-turner all weekend at the show. Robb had a handful of rideable prototypes on hand and reached out before the festival to see if I wanted to go for a ride. While the design and aesthetics are polarizing, my curiosity was piqued. As I continue to die on the hill, screaming “stack height is too low” into the wind, how could I ignore Robb’s solution to stack height inequity?

Essentially, ASYM bikes decouple stack height and reach from overall frame size and wheelbase. This allows for someone who would need an XL fit to ride a smaller, say, medium, wheelbase. ASYM bikes achieve this through a linkage bonded to the head tube of the bike, giving the frame greater reach and stack measurement while not sizing up the overall frame size.

I know a loooooot of people will say, just put a longer stem on it; what’s the big deal? Maintaining the familiar feel of a shorter stem and wide bars keeps the bike from the unwanted steering characteristics of a long stem. All the extra effort of bonding the second head tube and engineering the linkage that makes the ASYM bike work can feel overengineered just to avoid a long stem. While that could be true, I believe ASYM’s design opens a new conversation in bike fit and geometry where we can isolate certain measurements and have greater control over bike fit.

I took one of the prototypes on the same loop as every production bike on this list, and out of the gate I was so impressed with the linkage Robb has designed. The linkage had zero, and I mean zero, slop in the mechanism. It was smooth as butter, and if you didn’t look down, you would be unaware of all the engineering behind your bars. The 800+mm stack was instantly a treat, and I felt vindicated in my yelling from the hill I’ve been dying on. The bike rode impressively well considering how odd the front end looked. I never felt like I was going over the bars or had an issue controlling the bike.

I quickly thought of how many people bemoan 29-in wheels vs. 26-in for handling and playfulness. One could have the playful wheelbase of a smaller bike and the fit for however long, tall, or large you may be. My second thought was folks with back issues, as the ASYM mechanism adds so much stack height over a traditional bike. This could help people avoid sketchy stem extenders or excessive stems not rated for trail use.

Robb is passionate about his design and the benefits it can afford the right rider. I loved the extra stack height, and despite how visually odd the whole bike looked, the ride was both comfortable and capable. Reach out to him if you have any questions or might be interested in an ASYM for yourself!

This one was a double date with Robb and a few of his fleet. Things are developing slowly, but I’d be interested in a second date, given the passion behind the engineering.

Canfield Tilt V3 

  • 141 mm rear travel, 140 mm fork travel
  • Adjustable rear travel via shock stroke
    • 210×52.5 mm: 135 mm
    • 210×50 mm: 128 mm
    • 210×55 mm: 141 mm (as ridden)
  • Three chainstay positions (427 / 435 / 442 mm)
  • Recommended fork: 130–150 mm (optimized around 140 mm)
  • Patented Canfield Balance Formula™ (CBF™) suspension
  • 7005 aluminum frame with CNC 7075 T6 links

The Canfield Tilt V3 was the most versatile bike I pedaled over the weekend, with adjustable chainstay lengths and adaptability for three shock strokes to adjust travel. I was curious to try a Canfield Balance Formula-equipped bike that was not carbon for my first time trying the Formula. I love aluminum, and as such, I find myself drawn to the thick welds and industrial aesthetic of the Canfields. While the Brat green color was striking, I love that Canfield offers their bikes in raw aluminum, the best way to let aluminum show off.

The Tilt V3 pedaled as efficiently as the CBF formula promises and delivers equal plush suspension when you point it downhill. Even being a mid-travel aluminum bike with metal wheels, the bike was lively and decidedly non-puggy. Being a demo, it had a bit too much seatpost and a depressing lack of stack height for an XL frame. I would go on a second date with the Canfield Tilt V3 if it had a 210×50 mm shock, 50 mm riser bars, and a raw frame.

Revel Ranger Ti

  • 120 mm rear travel, 130 mm fork travel
  • Titanium front triangle
  • Carbon rear triangle and linkage
  • Shared geometry and kinematics with Ranger V3 Carbon

The belle of the ball for the weekend! Everyone had eyes for this stunning mix of titanium and carbon. Pulling together all the material expertise Revel has accumulated over the years into a singular bike is as impressive as it is expensive. Though I heard they have been selling quite well…

After my first foray with the CBF kinematics on the Canfield, I got to sample Revel’s version of the Formula. I would need to spend more time to develop a more nuanced take on the differences between each brand’s implementations of the system. The Ranger pedals with a calm demeanor and delivers plush suspension on the downhill. Revel only had a size large at the event, and seeing as I doubt this will be available for review, I took my chance, ill-fitting as it was.

The Ti Ranger is for the connoisseur of short travel trail bikes. For a rider who can appreciate the elegant flex of a titanium frame, one who prefers jazz-lines over plowing. Had I a million dollars (~$6k for a frame) and a fine bottle of zinfandel, I would take the Revel Ranger Ti on a second date, but it would need some platforms to be a proper XL frame. A second date would be nice.

Spot Diggity 125

  • 125 mm rear travel, 130 mm fork travel
  • Carbon frame
  • Living Link Titanium plate lower linkage

Hot diggity dog, I was excited to throw my leg over the refined Living Link-equipped diggity. I had a really fun time riding the poppiest of the poppy, Spot Ryve, a few years ago. The titanium plate lower link of the Living Link system provides active energy return on compression, giving Spot bikes a lively, active suspension feel.

Out of the gate, I have to say that I believe the Diggity climbed even better than either of the CBF bikes I rode over the weekend. They all were very, very impressive, but the Diggity squeaked ahead in the climbing department. Finally getting to ride a proper XL after a slew of large frames, presented adequate (it’s never enough) stack and reach to stretch out briefly. I have found Spot bikes to be very dependent on rebound adjustment due to the Living Link suspension. Initially, the bike felt harsh on square impacts, but a quick 2 clicks on the rebound adjustment and the Diggity was feeling almost as plush as the Revel Ranger Ti.

I had a lovely date with the Diggity, and it was the bike I felt most endeared to throughout the weekend. The newer suspension layout is more mild-mannered than the Ryve, in a good way; I pedaled a few years ago. I had such a lovely time with the Diggity that I don’t feel like I would need a second date, likewise in a good way.

Trek Superfly 32

  • 110 mm rear travel, 120 mm fork travel
  • 32″ wheels, ZOMG
  • Carbon frame
  • Details about the frame and components are unreleased

While the Revel Ranger Ti was the belle of the ball, the Trek Superfly prototype was the bike everyone wanted to dance with over the weekend. I secured a reservation first thing Sunday morning before I had to head home. I was glad to have a full 32″, full-suspension experience as my last bike for the weekend, so it would not taint my experience of the other lesser-wheeled-diameter bikes. Details were scarce and embargoed on the new Superfly. The suspension bears the mark of Fox’s RAD (Racing Application Development), signifying the bit’s prototype nature.

My curiosity about the Superfly was the feasibility of a full-suspension 32″ platform rather than the specimen itself. I have no need for, nor a proper opinion on, a world-class XC rig when all is said and done, but being 6’1″, I have to be intrigued by the prospect of a proportional XC bike. Trek only had a large frame, but due to the 32″ wheels and despite the negative rise stem, which I hate with the fiery passion of a thousand suns for taking away the prospect of proper stack height, it was actually fairly comfortable.

As far as I can tell, the geo and fork offsets remain similar to 29″ counterparts and thus feel familiar overall. The Superfly was noticeably smoother through chunder and dodged hangups in rock gardens better than any of the 29″ bikes I pedaled. Riding 32″ Aspens feels like riding 29+ Chronicles at the inception of the last large wheel revolution, in the worst way. Them Aspens do go fast, and I found myself scrubbing speed many times where I had simply coasted by on other bikes. I was likewise unencumbered on tight climbs and descents by the larger wheels.

No one needs to run out and buy a 32″ bike, but if you are already in the market for an XC bike in the future and you happen to be tall, I don’t see any reason to fight the new wheel size. I had far more fun on our date than I would have expected, a wonderful way to cap off a fun weekend of speed dating. I won’t be having a second date with a Trek Superfly, but I do look forward to meeting its other 32″ cousins in the future…
